title: kv-cache-block-allocator-compaction-notes
content:
Overview:
This note captures an alternate approach to the KV cache memory design that focuses on block-based allocation + online compaction for long-lived GPU-resident KV entries. The intent is to reduce fragmentation without resorting to aggressive global slab rebalancing. This is intentionally a practical / working doc with experiments and heuristics we can iterate on.

Goals:
- Keep per-request tail latency predictable for chat/generation workloads (strict p99 SLO)
- Minimize peak GPU memory waste from fragmentation (target <6% lost space after warmup)
- Support mixed-size KV entries (32B small keys up to multi-MB KV blobs for very long contexts)
- Allow background compaction that doesn't block hot allocation paths
- Provide simple tunables for Dedicated/Private customers (less aggressive compaction for constrained CPUs)

Constraints & assumptions:
- Most entries are medium-sized (1KB–128KB) for open models with extended contexts. Small entries <256B are relatively rare but latency-sensitive.
- We must support pinned entries (for beam search / generation checkpoints) that cannot be moved without invalidating references.
- GPU memory copies are expensive; minimize device-to-device and host-device transfers during normal ops.
- Allocation path must be lock-light for high concurrency; per-thread or per-stream caches are allowed.

High-level design summary (novelty):
We allocate KV entries from fixed-size contiguous blocks (4MiB default) that are grouped into arenas. Each arena maps to a physical region in GPU memory (or host mapped pinned memory for Private mode). Within a block we use an embedded mini-buddy allocator for small fragments and a free-segment list for larger holes. Blocks maintain a small header with metadata (bitmap for allocated fragments, live-bytes counter, fragmentation score).

Key ideas that differ from existing slab/bucket designs:
- Block compaction instead of global slab merging: when a block's fragmentation score exceeds threshold, we schedule it for compaction: live entries are migrated out to a new block and the source block becomes contiguous free space. Compaction is block-local and can be executed concurrently on multiple blocks.
- Hot/cold block classification: track access frequency per-entry and keep weighted counts per-block. Blocks with high heat are pinned from compaction; cold blocks are first candidates.
- Eviction integrates compaction: before evicting a set of entries we attempt to free space via intra-block compaction (moving surviving entries) to preserve higher-value entries. This reduces churn on the eviction set.

Block layout (4MiB example):
- Block header (aligned) ~4KB: epoch, version, live_count, live_bytes, frag_score, block_heat, lockflag
- Metadata region ~32KB: slot directory for entries (entry id -> offset/length/flags) optimized for vectorized scans
- Payload region ~remaining bytes: entries stored contiguously after compaction; fragmentation manifests as free holes between used ranges when entries are freed in-place.

Allocation strategy within a block:
- Small allocs (<1KB): use fixed mini-buddy within block to avoid per-entry metadata overhead.
- Medium allocs (1KB–128KB): appended into payload if space at tail; otherwise reuse freed holes tracked by a segregated free list (by size class).
- Large allocs (>128KB): allocated as dedicated contiguous runs (may span blocks if contiguous space isn't available) — large runs are placed into a "large-object" arena to avoid polluting small-block fragmentation.

Fragmentation detection and scoring:
We compute a block fragmentation score every N updates (N ~ 4096 ops) using:
frag_score = 1 - (largest_free_segment / total_free_bytes) * (1 - small_hole_penalty)
Where small_hole_penalty emphasizes many tiny holes. The metric aims to identify blocks with many small unusable holes even if total free bytes looks OK. Thresholds: schedule compaction when frag_score > 0.65 and total_free_bytes / block_size > 0.12.

Compaction flow (online):
- Candidate block is placed on a compaction queue. Worker threads pull blocks and try to compact.
- Block locked for writes (lock is cooperative; readers get epoch-based view so they can continue to access entries during migration; write/replace operations stall briefly).
- Live entries are copied to target block (preferably a freshly allocated block in same arena). During copy we update a pending-migration table mapping old offsets -> new offsets.
- After all entries copied, atomically swap block metadata to point to new layout and release old buffer as free. Readers racing on moved entries consult the pending table; if they see a migration in progress they can either: retry, or access the old data until the final commit. We prefer the latter for low-latency reads.
- Pinned entries are excluded; if a block contains many pinned entries (>40%) we skip compaction and mark block as long-term.

Eviction integration:
- Eviction candidates are selected by a combined score: eviction_score(entry) = alpha * recency_rank + beta * size_cost + gamma * estimated_recreate_cost.
- Before evicting M bytes, try compaction target on blocks that hold many eviction candidates to consolidate free space. If compaction frees sufficient contiguous run, we evict fewer entries.
- For multi-tenant/dedicated customers we expose a policy to favor model-isolation: prefer to evict low-priority tenant entries first and optionally throttle cross-tenant compaction to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

Memory pools / arenas:
- Per-model arenas: each top-level model (and optionally model+variant) gets a logical arena to avoid cross-model fragmentation. This is the default for Dedicated.
- Shared arena: for small sessions / transient entries, a shared arena allows reuse across models and reduces cold-start memory pressure.
- Large-object arena: dedicated for >128KB entries to avoid large-copy churn in small blocks.
- CPU-backed pinned arena: for Private mode where GPU memory is constrained, we maintain host-pinned shadow pages; cold entries can be migrated off-device by background movers (tradeoff: higher latency on read).

Performance considerations / micro-optimizations:
- Keep block headers cache-line aligned and <64 bytes read hot for the common allocator path.
- Use per-thread allocation caches that pull an active block to avoid contention; release the block if idle for 100ms.
- Compaction workers run at lower CPU priority; rate-limit copies per-second to avoid starving latency-critical inference.
- Prefer device-to-device memcpy (cudaMemcpyAsync) for GPU local compaction; if not available fall back to host staging.

Metrics to track:
- Block fragmentation distribution histogram (percent of blocks in 0–1 frag buckets)
- Average and p99 malloc latency (per-size-class)
- Bytes reclaimed by compaction vs bytes freed by eviction
- Compaction throughput (MB/s) and CPU cost
- Number of pinned blocks and pinned entry ratio
- Tail-latency impact during compaction windows (p99 request latency for model under compaction)

API and telemetry changes:
- Add admin endpoints: /kv/arenas/{id}/fragmentation and /kv/compaction/trigger (manual trigger with mode: aggressive|balancing|light)
- Expose per-model tuning knobs: compaction_threshold, large_object_cutoff, pinned_ratio_limit
- Add events for compaction start/finish, block-migration-failure, and forced-eviction-due-to-fragmentation

Rollout plan (phased):
1) Internal canary: enable block compaction read-only telemetry (no migration) to observe frag stats (2 weeks)
2) Canary compaction on non-critical models with low QPS; rate limit compaction workers (4 weeks)
3) Broader rollout with telemetry and per-tenant opt-out (6 weeks)
4) GA with API knobs and default conservative thresholds (quarterly)

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- Migration visibility semantics: allow readers to read old buffer until commit vs immediate redirect. The former is lower latency but a small window where writes might be lost or require CAS.
- Optimal block size: 4MiB is a heuristic. Larger blocks reduce header overhead but increase cost of copying during compaction. Need benchmarks for 1MiB/2MiB/8MiB.
- Cost model for estimated_recreate_cost in eviction_score: should include model tokenizer cost, partial decode, and expected future hits (hard to estimate).
- Interaction with KV persistence (cold-store): when compaction moves entries across arenas, should we update the persistence pointers? Keep it simple for now: persistence keyed by entry id, not by location.

Action items / next experiments:
- [ ] Microbench: measure compaction cost for 4MiB vs 1MiB blocks using synthetic mix (distribution attached in GH-rl/kv-allocator PR #478)
- [ ] Implement frag_score telemetry and histograms in canary cluster
- [ ] Build a background compaction prototype that uses epoch-based reader snapshots (Maya + Ethan)
- [ ] Validate host-pinned shuffle path for Private mode in limited testbed (Luca)

Notes-to-self / rough ideas:
- Consider a hybrid: slab for very small objects (<256B), block allocator for everything else.
- If compaction too expensive, consider adaptive threshold that only compacts when eviction rate exceeds expected baseline.

References:
- GH-rl/kv-allocator: PR #478 (proto code & microbench)
- JIRA R-INF-912: KV cache compaction epic
- Slack: #serving-runtime pinned thread: kv-cache-defrag

This doc is intentionally pragmatic and focuses on an in-place block compaction model that should be easier to reason about than global slab rebalance. Feedback welcome — particularly on the frag_score metric and the safety model for reader visibility during migration.
